extracted.intended_audience: aspiring travel writers, essayists, memoirists, and general prose writers
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative guidance for composing travelogues, memoirs, biographies, and character sketches — what to include, what to avoid, and how to interest and benefit readers. Emphasises human life, useful particulars, and narrative incident over trivial cataloguing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose: instruct, please, or both
rubrics_metrics.description: Every writer of travels (and writers generally) undertakes either to instruct or please, or to mingle pleasure with instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you instruct, 'offer to the mind something to be imitated, or something to be avoided.' If you please, 'offer new images to his reader, and enable him to form a tacit comparison of his own state with that of others.' Decide the primary aim and shape material accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on human life and usefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: The great object of remark in travel writing is human life: 'Every nation has something peculiar in its manufactures, its works of genius, its medicines, its agriculture, its customs and its policy.' A useful traveller 'brings home something by which his country may be benefited; who procures some supply of want, or some mitigation of evil...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise observations that inform readers about peoples' practices, institutions, and ways of life that can be compared to, learned from, or used to improve the reader's own society. Avoid idle scenic description that lacks human or practical consequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid empty general accounts and indistinct descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Many travel narratives disappoint because they contain either 'general accounts as leave no distinct idea behind them' or 'minute enumerations as few can read with either profit or delight.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not produce vague summaries that leave no clear impression. Instead of saying a place is 'green' or 'sandy', give specific, memorable images or human particulars. Avoid listlike, bland summaries that fail to create distinct ideas in the reader's mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid tedious minute enumerations, catalogues, and transcriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticised are writers who 'amuse the gentle reader with catalogues of pictures', 'recount the number of the pillars or variegations of the pavement', or 'copy inscriptions... and transcribe into their book the walls of every edifice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not catalogue artworks, architectural features, inscriptions, or routine itinerary details (hour-by-hour marches, streams likely dry in summer) unless they serve a human or thematic purpose. Use selective, meaningful detail rather than exhaustive inventory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not infer peoples' manners from trivial accommodations
rubrics_metrics.description: It is misleading to 'guess at the manners of the inhabitants by the entertainment which his inn afforded him.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid making broad cultural claims based on single, incidental observations (e.g., the quality of an inn). Ground judgments in repeated, corroborated social observations or in explicit interactions with inhabitants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stay long enough and engage enough to produce useful observation
rubrics_metrics.description: The common failing is superficial travelling: entering a town at night, surveying it in the morning, and hastening away produces little that can be told.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immersion and longer observation are necessary to gather reliable material. If your method of travelling 'supplies him with nothing to be told', do not try to write as if you had deep knowledge; instead linger, investigate, and seek human particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memoir/biography: include incidents, distress, and vicissitudes
rubrics_metrics.description: For lives and memoirs, 'nothing detains the reader's attention more powerfully than deep involutions of distress, or sudden vicissitudes of fortune' — the gradations of an author's life are 'from book to book.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing memoir or biography, foreground turning points, crises, reversals, major projects (books) and their consequences, and the emotional and social effects of success and failure. These create narrative shape and reader interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show gradual changes and progressions (trace developments over time)
rubrics_metrics.description: Useful biographical detail includes 'the gradations of a patron, traced from the first glow which flattery raises... to the last chill look of final dismission.' 'The gradations of a hero's life are from battle to battle, and of an author's from book to book.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict relations, reputations, fortunes, and habits as processes. Trace how opinions, patronage, favor, or habits evolve rather than presenting static judgments. Chronological sequences and comparative episodes make patterns visible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character sketches through habitual, concrete details
rubrics_metrics.description: Character is best conveyed by recurring, specific behaviors and small particulars (example: Miss Gentle's punctuality, needlework schedule, cautious conversation, patterned laughter, and the watch that governs her time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show character through consistent, observable actions, routines, and reactions (what a person does at a certain minute, how they laugh, what they forgive or resent). Avoid abstract labeling; let habits illustrate traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overreaching claims or making a show of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: A warning against recording or claiming knowledge one cannot truly have: 'Why should he record excursions by which nothing could be learned, or wish to make a show of knowledge, which, without some power of intuition unknown to other mortals, he never could attain?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about grand generalizations or authoritative statements based on insubstantial observation. Limit claims to what your evidence supports, or qualify them honestly.
